dell26.text_read: abstract only (Crossref record; fetch tool paraphrased, no verbatim quote longer than tool limit)
key_findings: Abstract (paraphrased by fetch tool): preregistered experiment, 758 BCG knowledge workers; arms no AI / GPT-4 / GPT-4 + prompt-engineering overview
On 18 tasks inside the frontier, AI users completed more tasks, faster, with higher quality
On a task outside the frontier, AI users were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions (abstract wording per tool: '19% less likely')
"However, generative AI–enabled stories are more similar to each other than stories by humans alone."
Abstract (paraphrased): stories written with AI ideas rated more creative, better written, more enjoyable, largest gains for less creative writers; framed as a social dilemma

diet15.text_read: full text (author PDF, Wharton faculty site; abstract and overview checked via fetch tool)
key_findings: "more quickly lose confidence in algorithmic than human forecasters after seeing them make the same mistake"
"even when they see them outperform a human forecaster"
"regardless of whether the human forecaster is the participant herself or another, anonymous participant"
Tasks: MBA-student percentile forecasts (Studies 1, 2, 4); state airline-passenger ranks (Studies 3a, 3b)
"lay people adhere more to advice when they think it comes from an algorithm than from a person"
tasks: "numeric estimates about a visual stimulus" and "forecasts about the popularity of songs and romantic attraction"
"experienced professionals, who make forecasts on a regular basis, relied less on algorithmic advice than lay people did, which hurt their accuracy"
"algorithms are trusted and relied on less for tasks that seem subjective"

Abstract (paraphrased): raising perceived task objectivity, or algorithms' perceived humanlike affective ability, increases reliance; 4 online lab studies (>1,400) and 2 online field studies (>56,000)

issues: Scene says 'A firm gives professionals an AI assistant'; the study was a preregistered online experiment with randomized ChatGPT access, not a firm deployment. Numbers (453, 40%, 18%) are correct.

corrections.scene: In an online experiment, 453 professionals complete short occupation-specific writing tasks; half are randomly given access to ChatGPT.

ai01.evidence: Abstract: "The average time taken decreased by 40% and output quality rose by 18%." (Crossref abstract)

ai02.evidence: Abstract: "output quality rose by 18%." Chart 100->118 consistent. Grading by evaluators is consistent with 'externally evaluated' (detail from paper design, not re-read in full text).

ai03.evidence: Abstract: "increases worker productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 15% on average"; less experienced and lower-skilled workers gained most.

ai04.evidence: Abstract: 5,172 agents; "issues resolved per hour, by 15% on average." Chart 100->115 consistent.

issues: Minor: scene implies each consultant did several tasks across the frontier; design had an inside-frontier task set (18 tasks) and a separate outside-frontier task. Not misleading for the policy question.
ai05.evidence: Crossref abstract (paraphrased): AI improved quantity, speed and quality on 18 tasks inside the frontier; AI users less likely to be correct on the task outside it.

issues: Title 'When expertise backfires' is loose: the paper shows AI use backfiring outside the frontier, not human expertise backfiring. Consider 'When AI help backfires'.
ai06.evidence: Crossref abstract: AI helps on some tasks and hurts on others within the same workflow; outside-frontier task correctness fell for AI users.

ai07.evidence: Abstract: AI-idea stories rated more creative; "generative AI–enabled stories are more similar to each other than stories by humans alone."

issues: Applied extrapolation to campaign concepts; scene is hypothetical and explain correctly attributes the tension to the story experiment.
Scene says the model outperforms 'a human expert'; in the studies the human forecaster was the participant herself or another anonymous participant, not an expert.

corrections.scene: A prediction model outperforms a human forecaster but makes visible errors.

ai09.evidence: "regardless of whether the human forecaster is the participant herself or another, anonymous participant"; abstract: "even when they see them outperform a human forecaster" (Wharton author PDF).

issues: Boundary could note the paper's own exception: experienced forecasting professionals relied less on algorithmic advice.
ai10.evidence: "lay people adhere more to advice when they think it comes from an algorithm than from a person" (RePEc abstract).

ai11.evidence: "algorithms are trusted and relied on less for tasks that seem subjective" (Crossref abstract).

ai13.evidence: "more quickly lose confidence in algorithmic than human forecasters after seeing them make the same mistake" (abstract, Wharton PDF).

issues: 'improved evaluated story quality' is fine (rated more creative, better written, more enjoyable).
ai14.evidence: Abstract: more creative/better written; more similar to each other.

ai15.evidence: Abstract (paraphrased): gains largest for less experienced and lower-skilled agents, minimal for the most experienced.
